researchIntro: Recent and landmark studies in plain English, with the caveats that matter for a home lawn. Many come from university turf programs in the central U.S.; the findings on mowing, feeding and watering apply to the same grasses anywhere. Every citation was checked against its DOI.

local.name: Your state's Cooperative Extension
local.what: Every state has a land-grant university Extension service with county offices. They run soil tests, answer lawn and garden questions, and publish planting calendars and pest alerts for your state.
local.where: Find your state and county office

local.name: Extension Master Gardener help desks
local.what: Trained volunteers answer home garden questions for free by phone, email or at a walk-in desk, usually through the county Extension office.

local.name: USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map
local.what: Look up the hardiness zone for any ZIP code. The zone tells you which perennials, shrubs and trees survive your winters.

local.name: Call 811 before you dig
local.what: A free service that marks buried gas, power, water and cable lines before you dig for a tree, fence post or bed. Call or go online a few working days ahead.

local.name: State forestry nurseries
local.what: Many state forestry agencies sell bare-root native tree and shrub seedlings at low cost. Orders usually open in fall and ship in late winter and spring.
local.where: Search for your state's forestry or conservation department nursery

local.name: Native plant societies
local.what: State native plant societies list plants native to your region, the nurseries that sell them and local plant sales.
local.where: Search for your state's native plant society

suppliers.name: Independent garden centers
suppliers.what: Regionally suited plants, seed blends chosen for your climate, and staff who know local conditions.

suppliers.name: Farm and feed stores
suppliers.what: Bulk grass seed, fertilizer in 50-lb bags, straw, fencing and soil-test kits, usually at the lowest price per pound.

suppliers.name: Landscape supply yards
suppliers.what: Professional herbicides and fertilizers, bulk compost, mulch and topsoil by the cubic yard, with delivery.

suppliers.name: SiteOne Landscape Supply
suppliers.what: Professional-grade fertilizer, seed and herbicides; open to homeowners at most branches.

suppliers.name: Johnny's Selected Seeds
suppliers.what: Vegetable seed with detailed growing data and disease-resistance codes.

suppliers.name: DoMyOwn
suppliers.what: Professional lawn products in homeowner sizes, with labels posted for every product.

suppliers.name: Big-box home centers
suppliers.what: Common fertilizers, spreaders, mulch and tools. Read seed tags carefully; many bagged mixes are not suited to every region.

myths.myth: Water the lawn a little every day in summer.
myths.fact: Daily sprinkles grow shallow roots and disease. Soak ½–1 in only when needed (the 3-week rule), early in the morning.

myths.myth: A brown lawn in summer is dead.
myths.fact: Most lawn grasses go dormant and recover; in K-State trials tall fescue came back after 60–83 days with no water. Tug-test it before you panic.

myths.myth: Spring is the time to fertilize.
myths.fact: For tall fescue it's fall. In K-State plots, spring and May nitrogen went with 48–66% brown patch vs 2–23% for a September-only feeding.

myths.myth: A spring weed-and-feed takes care of everything.
myths.fact: Broadleaf weeds die best in fall, crabgrass preventer needs precise timing, and the lawn doesn't need April nitrogen. Combo products do each job at the wrong time.
Sand plus clay makes a concrete-like mix. Compost and core aeration are the fix.
Only in sodium-affected soils, which most garden soils aren't. Spend the money on compost instead.

myths.myth: Grub control gets rid of moles.
myths.fact: Moles eat mostly earthworms. Trapping is the reliable fix.

myths.myth: Japanese beetle traps protect my roses.
myths.fact: Traps attract far more beetles than they catch (University of Kentucky research; MU agrees). Hand-pick instead.

myths.myth: Blossom-end rot means the soil needs calcium (or Epsom salt).
myths.fact: Usually it's uneven watering; low soil calcium is rarely the cause. Mulch, water evenly, and test before adding anything.

myths.myth: Rhizomatous tall fescue will fill in bare spots.
myths.fact: K-State measured RTF rhizomes at about 3 mm vs 80+ mm for bluegrass. Reseed bare spots.

myths.myth: No Mow May is proven to help bees.
myths.fact: The study behind it was retracted in 2022. Mowing every 2–3 weeks and planting flowers does help (Lerman 2018).
Only if the soil is acidic. MU says to lime lawns only at pH 5.8 or lower, so test first.

myths.myth: Bag the clippings to prevent thatch.
myths.fact: Clippings break down fast and return nitrogen; tall fescue rarely builds thatch.

myths.myth: Seed in spring and put down crabgrass preventer at the same time.
myths.fact: Most preventers stop grass seed too. Seed in September; in spring use only mesotrione (Tenacity) or siduron at seeding.
A 2024 study found no consistent drought benefit. Choose cultivars with good NTEP data instead.

myths.myth: KY-31 is just as good and cheaper.
myths.fact: It's a 1943 pasture grass: coarse and clumpy. It scored 4.4 in NTEP's 2018 test vs 6.3–6.4 for the best turf types.
Many consumer Roundup products no longer contain glyphosate, or contain only a little. Read the active ingredient on the label, not the brand name.

myths.myth: Mulch piled around a tree protects it.
myths.fact: Mulch against the trunk rots bark and invites rodents and girdling roots. Make a flat donut, 2–3 in deep.

dataCredits: Weather, soil temperature and evapotranspiration: [Open-Meteo](https://open-meteo.com/) (free, no key).
Local climate and frost dates: estimated for your location from Open-Meteo's historical archive (ERA5 reanalysis), calibrated against NOAA NCEI U.S. Climate Normals 1991–2020.
ZIP code lookup: [Zippopotam.us](https://www.zippopotam.us/). Hardiness zones: USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map (2023) via [phzmapi.org](https://phzmapi.org/).
Planting windows: University of Missouri Extension G6201, moved to your frost dates. Vegetable varieties: K-State Research and Extension L41 and other state Extension lists.
Warm-season lawn care: NC State TurfFiles, Clemson HGIC, Texas A&M AggieTurf and UF/IFAS.
Lawn cultivar data: National Turfgrass Evaluation Program (NTEP) 2018 National Tall Fescue Test.
Heading font: Fraunces by the Fraunces Project Authors (SIL Open Font License 1.1). Icons drawn for this site.
